definition: A request header expressing which response media types a client can accept.
A response name assigned to a selected GraphQL field, useful for repeated selections with different arguments.
A JSON Schema condition requiring a value to satisfy every listed subschema.
A JSON Schema condition requiring a value to match at least one listed subschema.
A defined interface through which software requests capabilities or data from another component.
The agreed operations, inputs, outputs, constraints, errors, and behavior a consumer can rely on.
A credential or application identifier whose exact permissions and security properties depend on the API.
Structured documentation of individual operations and data elements, usually optimized for lookup.
Establishing the identity or credentials of an actor.
Deciding whether an actor may perform an action on a particular resource or field.
Increasing the delay between retries to reduce repeated load and avoid immediate repeated failures.
The common scheme, host, and path prefix used by a group of API operations.
A credential whose possession enables its use; protect it because another holder may be able to act with it.
A change that can invalidate a previously supported consumer interaction or assumption.
A domain condition beyond basic shape, such as allowing a return only for a delivered order.
HTTP directives that govern caching behavior for requests or responses.
Documentation that develops understanding of why and how a system behaves.
A request whose processing depends on supplied conditions, such as a matching representation validator.
A pagination convention typically exposing edges and pageInfo; it is not required for every GraphQL list.
A rule limiting valid data, such as a maximum length or an integer range.
Selection of a response representation using request preferences and server capabilities.
A header identifying the media type of the associated representation.
Checking that requests, responses, or behavior agree with the documented machine-readable contract.
Browser-enforced rules governing whether frontend code can read cross-origin responses; it is not an API authorization system.
An opaque continuation value whose interpretation and validity are controlled by the server.
A value or behavior applied when an input is omitted, if the implementation or contract defines one.
An HTTP method requesting removal of the target resource association; repeat responses may differ despite idempotent intent.
A notice discouraging use of an element while it remains available, normally with a replacement and policy.
The quality of the end-to-end experience of discovering, integrating, testing, and maintaining an API.
GraphQL syntax that modifies interpretation or execution at allowed locations, such as @include.
OpenAPI metadata that helps associate a payload discriminator value with a schema; it does not replace validation semantics.
Maintaining documentation through text sources, version control, review, automated checks, and repeatable builds.
A connection item containing a node and often a cursor or relationship metadata.
A callable interface location, often described by an HTTP method and path in REST references.
A defined set of named allowed values, such as IN_STOCK and OUT_OF_STOCK.
An opaque validator associated with a representation, used in conditional requests.
An illustrative or observed instance; it is not automatically a default or exhaustive specification.
A platform-specific approach to composing and executing a graph across separately managed schemas or services.
A reusable or inline GraphQL selection constrained by a type condition.
An HTTP method for retrieving a selected representation with safe, idempotent semantics.
A typed query language and execution model in which clients select fields from a schema.
A method like GET that returns response metadata without response content.
Task-oriented instructions for a reader who already understands the relevant concepts.
An application-layer protocol with request methods, response statuses, headers, and representation semantics.
HTTP protected by TLS, providing transport confidentiality and integrity with authenticated server identity when correctly configured.
The property that repeating an identical request has the same intended server effect as making it once.
A client-supplied identifier that an operation can use to detect and replay the same request intent under documented rules.
A GraphQL type used for structured operation inputs rather than returned object fields.
A GraphQL abstract type declaring fields that implementing object types must provide.
GraphQL's schema-inspection capability, used by tools to discover types and descriptions when enabled.
A text data format with objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null.
A vocabulary and processing model for describing and validating JSON instances.
A compact claims representation that may be signed or encrypted; using a JWT does not by itself establish a safe authentication design.
Task-oriented instructions for adapting an integration to changed behavior or contracts.
An integer subdivision of a currency; this demo uses 100 INR minor units per rupee, not a universal currency rule.
A GraphQL operation for changes, with serial execution of top-level mutation fields but no automatic transaction guarantee.
A pattern where resolving a list causes an additional dependent lookup per item, potentially increasing work substantially.
The business object within a connection edge, or a separately defined interface in some schema conventions.
A GraphQL wrapper that disallows null at a position and affects error propagation when resolution fails.
The movement of an execution failure upward through non-null positions until a nullable boundary can hold null.
Permitting null as a value; this is different from permitting a field to be absent.
An authorization framework for obtaining limited access to resources; it is not by itself a user-authentication protocol.
Selecting a collection portion by the number of matching items to skip and a limit.
A JSON Schema condition requiring a value to match exactly one listed subschema.
A standard language for describing HTTP APIs in a machine-readable document.
A unique identifier for an OpenAPI operation used by tooling and references.
A method used to describe communication options for a target; browser preflight is one use.
Connection metadata such as hasNextPage and endCursor used to continue traversal.
Dividing a collection into bounded portions with a documented way to continue.
A GraphQL result containing usable data alongside execution errors for other response positions.
An HTTP method for applying a partial modification according to the documented patch format and rules.
A variable embedded in a URL path, such as productId in /products/{productId}.
A GraphQL document stored or registered for reuse by identifier under a defined server policy.
An OAuth extension binding an authorization-code exchange to a client-generated verifier to mitigate code interception and related threats.
An HTTP method requesting resource-specific processing; its effects depend on the operation contract.
The RFC 9457 JSON or XML format for machine-readable HTTP API problem information with defined members and extensions.
An HTTP method whose intent is to create or replace the target resource state with the supplied representation.
A GraphQL operation intended to retrieve data through fields on the query root.
A named URL query value used for options such as filtering, sorting, or pagination.
A short, reproducible path to a first useful success with stated prerequisites and expected results.
A restriction on request or resource consumption over a defined scope and period.
A pointer to another schema or description component, avoiding repeated independent definitions.
Reusing a previously valid message or credential exchange to cause an unintended repeated action.
A transmitted description of a resource, such as a JSON product object.
The payload sent with a request, whose format is described by its media type.
Metadata sent with a request, such as Content-Type or Authorization.
A presence obligation at a specific location; it does not by itself determine whether null is accepted.
A concept identified and manipulated through an interface, such as a product or order.
Metadata returned with a response, such as ETag, Location, or Retry-After.
An architectural style with constraints including a uniform interface and stateless interactions; not every JSON-over-HTTP API fully follows it.
A response header that can communicate how long a client should wait before a follow-up request.
A method whose defined semantics are essentially read-only from the client's perspective.
A leaf GraphQL type; built-ins and custom scalars have specific serialization and input-coercion behavior.
A machine-readable definition of permitted data structure and constraints.
A named permission or access range whose meaning is defined by the authorization system.
GraphQL Schema Definition Language, the textual notation for types, fields, arguments, and related schema elements.
The fields requested at a GraphQL response position, including nested selections where required.
Subject-matter expert who can explain and review a specific area of product behavior.
A captured representation at a particular time; ShopVerse orders preserve line names and prices at creation.
The authoritative source for a fact; disagreements among implementation, contract, and intended behavior must be resolved.
An HTTP response code indicating the result category and semantics of the request handling.
A GraphQL operation model for results over time; a working service also needs a supported delivery transport.
A tool that renders OpenAPI descriptions into an interactive reference; it is not the OpenAPI specification itself.
A limit on waiting; it does not prove that a server-side write did not occur.
A learning-oriented sequence that builds understanding through a guided activity.
A GraphQL abstract type representing one of several object types without declaring shared business fields itself.
An address that identifies a resource location and may contain a scheme, host, path, query, and fragment.
A typed named input supplied separately from a GraphQL document, usually in JSON over HTTP.
A server-initiated HTTP notification sent to a configured receiver when a documented event occurs.
A structured data serialization format often used for human-edited API descriptions.
